1. In consequence of these different notions, all the different nations of Europe have studied, though to little purpose, every possible way of accumulating gold and silver in their respective countries. 

2. The great affair, we always find, is to get money. 

3. That wealth consists in money, or silver, is a popular notion which naturally arises from the double function of money, as the instrument of commerce and as the measure of value.

4. When that is obtained, there is no difficulty in making any subsequent purchase. 

5. In consequence of its being the instrument of commerce, when we have money we can more readily obtain whatever else we have occasion for than by means of any other commodity.

For over 2 million years, dire wolves roamed present-day North America until their extinction around 10,000 B.C. On Monday, a Dallas-based bioscience firm said it had brought the species back to life in the form of three pups, claiming to have “successfully restored a once-eradicated species through the science of de-extinction” in a remarkable statement on its website.

The team at Colossal said the pups were created using a combination of gene-editing techniques and ancient DNA found in fossils from between 11,500 and 72,000 years ago. Other scientists, however, say that while Colossal’s technological feats are impressive, the animals are not truly dire wolves — and that the process raises ethical questions. “The reality is we can’t de-extinct extinct creatures because we can’t use cloning — the DNA is just not well enough preserved,” said Nic Rawlence, an associate professor at University of Otago. ... “What Colossal is trying to do is genetically engineering animals to look like extinct creatures,” he said. ”

On Monday, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said he hoped de-extinction could lead to animals being removed from the endangered species list. Animal rights groups and scientists have argued, as de-extinction projects have increased in recent years, that the efforts should not replace traditional conservation methods. Diverting funding and focus from conservation to de-extinction could lead to more species being lost, one 2017 study published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution found. But Burgum said “the concept of ‘de-extinction’ can serve as a bedrock for modern species conservation.” “The status quo is focused on regulation more than innovation,” he added. “It’s time to fundamentally change how we think about species conservation.”

The “dire wolf” pups are the latest headline-grabbing claim from the bioscience venture which says it is working to bring back some of the world’s most famous extinct species, such as the woolly mammoth and the dodo [...] Some scientists are dismissive of the claims and wary of the company’s approach, even while expressing admiration for the technological accomplishments of its CRISPR gene editing techniques — in which a piece of DNA can be snipped out from a genome and precisely replaced. In the wolves’ case, scientists edited the gray wolf genome to approximate the size, color and coat of a dire wolf, Rawlence said. “Their technology is amazing, but my personal view is it needs to be used to conserve the animals we’ve got left,” he said. This could include using money the company has raised to manage existing endangered species or reintroduce genetic diversity among existing species to help them adapt to climate change or diseases.

He said trying to re-create the characteristics of extinct animals provides no incentive to conserve species and raises questions about where and how the animals will live. “Is there even going to be a habitat the animal can adapt to? How are you going to deal with increased human-wolf conflict? What’s going to happen when your genetically enginered gray wolves hybridize with other gray wolves?” he said. He also posed ethical considerations: Will extinction companies trademark these creatures? Who owns them? These are all discussions we need to have,” he said.

options.label: B

options.label: A

There is nothing duller than broad satire. If a widely held belief is satirised and mocked in a play, and no one comes to watch, is it still funny? [...] Satire relies on a bond of trust between the creator and the audience. The satirist assumes the audience understands the language and context he or she is working in and is not supposed to care if they don’t. The audience member trusts artists to be true to their visions, even at the expense of his or her own understanding of specific references. Once the satirist goes too broad to explain things or to make sure the audience is on board with the proceedings, the bond is broken. The deal is off. The vision is dispelled.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.option_text: Satire loses its impact when it tries to broadly appeal to everyone instead of trusting the audience to grasp its subtleties.

options.label: D
options.option_text: Satire thrives when there is trust between the audience and the artist, and the artist balances their vision with the breadth of the act.

questions.solution_text:
The passage argues that satire is most powerful when it remains true to the creator's vision and assumes a certain level of understanding from its audience. It suggests that effective satire depends on a mutual trust: the satirist trusts the audience to comprehend nuanced language and perhaps the cultural context, while the audience trusts the satirist not to compromise the work for accessibility. When a satirist broadens their approach to make sure everyone “gets it, they risk weakening the satire and breaking that essential bond. Option C accurately captures this idea. 
Option A is tempting, but the phrase “rendering satire futile” is too strong and oversimplifies the point; it also puts more emphasis on the breach of trust than on the satirical vision being compromised. Option B reframes the issue as a two-sided failure of expectations, which the passage does not necessarily emphasise; this shifts the focus away from the satirists’ motive of broadening “their approach.” Option D is also misleading since it suggests that the satirist should balance their vision with broad appeal, whereas the passage argues the opposite. 
Hence, Option C is the best choice.
